newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY C.BANK HEAD DENIES SACKINGS LINK TO SCANDAL.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY C.BANK HEAD DENIES SACKINGS LINK TO SCANDAL.

text.p: Hungary's central bank head on Tuesday denied any link between the resignations of two of his vice presidents over an options deal and a recent privatisation agency scandal over irregular payments to a consultant.
"A very deep and clear differentiation between this case and another case which occupies the public opinion must be made," National Bank of Hungary (NBH) president Gyorgy Suranyi told reporters.
"I am convinced that the prime minister's decision was not unaffected by the mood and circumstances among which we live now."

Harshegyi and fellow NBH vice president Sandor Czirjak offered their resignations after disclosure of an unfavourable foreign exchange contract with Creditanstalt Investment Fund, concluded in 1992, that could cost the NBH hundreds more than three billion forints.
The contract was for foreign exchange rate guarantees maturing in 1998 that forced the NBH to create substantial risk reserves that have proven extremely costly.

The news came hard on the heels of a scandal over a payments of millions of dollars paid by the state privatisation agency APV Rt to a consultant, Marta Tocsik. That revelation led to the dismissal of the entire APV board and the minister in charge.
Harshegyi on Monday told Reuters he was being wrongly singled out for one decision at the expense of his overall record.
"One should not be judged over one decision which may have a positive or negative effect but on one's overall performance," he said.
"I think he's right," said analyst Tibor Vidos of GJW Consult. "If this had come to light before the Tocsik affair nothing would have happened."
"They are victims in an indirect way as there is now a general intolerance against executives in the public sector."
Vidos said the general climate could eventually harm the image of the government abroad but that there were signs the worst may be over.
"The APV's new board is up and running and things are getting back to normal."
The government said on Monday the new board would hold its first meeting on Wednesday.

Vidos added that new privatisation minister Judit Csiha seemed more ready than her predecessor Tamas Suchman to allow the management to get on with its job. He also said new APV board chairman Arpad Kovacs's record as head of the State Audit Office would ensure that rules are adhered to.
Political analyst Attila Ledenyi said he believed the government was under pressure to take any whiff of scandal extremely seriously.
"The government feels it is important that people who make mistakes should resign so they overplayed this one. Otherwise it seems ridicilous to bring things up from years ago."
Ledenyi also beieved public interest in the scandal was waning and that Western investors were more concerned about consistent government policy.

"People are getting a little tired of the so-called Tocsik affair. After a while they stop listening, while investors know these things happen occasionally and would be more concerned of the government changed its (privatisation) policy, which it cleary is not."
The Hungarian Parliament on Tuesday confirmed Csiha as privatisation minister and Szabolcs Fazakas as the new minister of trade, industry and tourism to replace Suchman, who held both portfolios.
Csiha told reporters upon her appointment that she was determined that privatisation would continue interrupted.
"The government is determined that the process of privatisation must be continued," she said. "One cannot and should not expect a change in strategy which would weaken or reverse this philosophy."
She announced the setting up of a committee to examine all contracts entered into by APV.
"I have to make sure that decisions, decrees made by the parliament and government, are implemented."
Suranyi on Tuesday gave more details of the deal which had forced the Harshegyi amd Czirjak's resignation.

He said the NBH and an unnamed partner concluded an option deal in 1992, in which they shared forint devaluation risks, but the partner did not have to pay an option fee, which Suranyi called the main technical mistake.
The deal forced the NBH to create substantial risk reserves, and the lack of the option fee increased the loss of the central bank to hundreds of million forints.

Suranyi declined to estimate how much further loss is expected by the 1998 maturity of the contract, but said the vice presidents decision were only one of several other decisions which generated much larger profits for the central bank than the loss suffered due to the 1992 contract.

Suranyi said the vice presidents had contributed substantially to the improvement of the NBH's picture in Hungary and abroad and as such he had urged Prime Minister Gyula Horn not to accept their resignation.
"I recommended him not to accept the resignation offers, or at least not with an effect which is so close."
